expansion:
A. Keratoconus is correct. This vignette describes corneal ectasia: progressive thinning and protrusion producing irregular astigmatism and visual distortion. The lecture defines ectasia as conditions with “progressive corneal thinning & protrusion” that “cause irregular astigmatism,” and identifies keratoconus as the most common type (L15,16, page 22). It specifically describes keratoconus as progressive, often asymmetric corneal thinning and protrusion, with onset at puberty; “eye rubbing” and “atopy” are listed risk factors (L15,16, page 23). Thus, the boy’s age, severe atopy, habitual rubbing, progressive distortion, and irregular astigmatism point directly to keratoconus.

B. Corneal arcus is wrong. The lecture describes arcus senilis as an age-related “lipid arc at limbus,” physiological in elderly people, rather than a progressive ectatic disorder causing corneal thinning, protrusion, and irregular astigmatism (L15,16, page 29).

C. Band keratopathy is wrong. It is calcium deposition in Bowman’s layer in the interpalpebral zone and is associated with chronic ocular disease, hypercalcaemia, and chronic uveitis (L15,16, page 30). This is a corneal deposition disorder, not the thinning-and-protrusion process described in the stem.

D. Fuchs endothelial dystrophy is wrong. The lecture attributes it to abnormal endothelial cell function with loss of the dehydrating pump, guttata, and corneal oedema progressing to bullous keratopathy; characteristic vision is worse in the morning, and risk factors include older age in the 5th–6th decade (L15,16, page 28). That mechanism and demographic do not fit this adolescent with atopy and eye rubbing.
objective: Recognize keratoconus as progressive corneal ectasia causing thinning, protrusion, and irregular astigmatism, with eye rubbing and atopy as risk factors.
